title: You Want a Godly Spouse. Are You Becoming the Kind of Person Who Knows How to Love One?
paragraphs: You Want a Godly Spouse. Are You Becoming the Kind of Person Who Knows How to Love One?

Maybe God is doing something deeper in your waiting season than preparing someone for you. Maybe He is teaching you how to become someone who can love another human being without asking them to become what only Jesus can be.
You have prayed for them.
Maybe more times than you would admit.
“Lord, send me someone who loves You.”
Someone faithful.
Someone emotionally mature.
Someone who will pray with me.
Someone who understands commitment.
Someone who won’t play games with my heart.
Someone who will stay.
Someone who knows Scripture.
Someone who wants marriage, not situationships.
Someone who is serious about Jesus.
And there is nothing shameful about desiring that.
Marriage is not a dirty desire. Scripture presents marriage as honorable, and the longing to share your life with another person can be beautiful.

But somewhere between another wedding invitation, another engagement announcement on your screen, another “So, are you seeing anyone?” from a relative, and another night lying alone with your phone glowing beside you...
the desire can quietly become something else.
You stop merely wanting marriage.
You start believing marriage will finally make you whole.
And that is where a good desire can begin carrying a weight God never designed it to carry.
Because you can spend years asking God,
“Where is the right person?”
while God is confronting you with another question:
Are you becoming the kind of person who knows how to love one?
That question hurts differently.
Because it is easier to create a checklist for somebody else than to let Jesus examine us.
Faithful.
Kind.
Patient.
Pure.
Prayerful.
Emotionally available.
Humble.
Forgiving.
Gentle.
Spiritually mature.
We know what we want.
But imagine placing your own name at the top of the list.
Not theirs.
Yours.
Am I faithful?
Am I kind when I am disappointed?
Am I patient when I don't get what I want?
Can I apologize without defending myself?
Can I hear correction without turning cold?
Do I know how to forgive?
Can I disagree without humiliating someone?
Do I manipulate affection when I feel insecure?
Do I punish people with silence?
Do I demand reassurance because I have made another human being responsible for wounds I refuse to bring before Christ?
Do I know how to serve when nobody applauds me?
Do I know how to love someone when loving them costs me something?
Suddenly the prayer changes.
“God, send me the right person” becomes...
“Jesus, make me faithful.”
And maybe that is one of the holiest things that can happen in your waiting season.
Paul wrote to believers in Colossae:
“Put on therefore, as God’s elect, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering;
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.
And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.”
— Colossians 3:12–14, KJV
The original Greek makes Paul's language even more striking.
He begins with:
Ἐνδύσασθε οὖν — endýsasthe oun
“Therefore, clothe yourselves.”
The verb ἐνδύω — endýō carries the idea of putting on clothing.
Paul is describing something believers are called to intentionally wear because of who they already are in Christ.
Compassion.
Kindness.
Humility.
Gentleness.
Patience.
These are not merely traits you should search for on somebody's dating profile.
They are garments Christ calls you to put on.
Then comes a phrase that destroys romantic fantasy:
ἀνεχόμενοι ἀλλήλων — anechómenoi allḗlōn
“bearing with one another.”
That isn't particularly cinematic.
Nobody puts that on a Valentine's card.
Nobody posts engagement photographs with the caption:
“I finally found someone I will occasionally have to bear with.”
But Scripture understands something romantic culture often hides.
You will marry a sinner.
And if you marry, your spouse will marry one too.
You.
Marriage does not bring together two flawless Christians who have finally completed God's compatibility assessment.
It brings together two human beings who desperately need grace.
There will be mornings when neither person looks particularly spiritual.
There will be misunderstandings.
Stress.
Exhaustion.
Financial pressure.
Unspoken expectations.
Bad moods.
Old wounds.
Disappointments.
There may be moments when the person who once made your heart race becomes the person who tests your patience before breakfast.
That is why biblical love requires something deeper than chemistry.
Paul continues:
χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς — charizómenoi heautoîs
“forgiving one another.”
The verb χαρίζομαι — charízomai is related to χάρις — cháris:
grace.
Paul does not merely tell Christians to tolerate each other's imperfections.
He points them toward grace.
And then he gives the standard:
καθὼς καὶ ὁ Κύριος ἐχαρίσατο ὑμῖν
“as the Lord forgave you.”
There it is.
Jesus.
Christian relationships cannot ultimately be understood by staring endlessly at ourselves or our romantic expectations.
We look at Christ.
You want someone forgiving?
Look at Jesus.
You want someone patient?
Look at Jesus.
You want someone sacrificial?
Look at Jesus.
You want someone faithful?
Look at Jesus.
And then comes the uncomfortable part:
Follow Him.
Because Christianity is not primarily about finding somebody who resembles your ideal spouse.
It is about being transformed into the likeness of Christ.
This means singleness is not God's waiting room where your real life has not started yet.
Read that again.
Your life with Jesus is happening now.
You are not spiritually parked until somebody proposes.
You are not half a person waiting for your missing half.
Marriage is precious, but marriage is not your Messiah.
A husband cannot bear the weight of being your savior.
A wife cannot carry the burden of becoming your ultimate source of identity.
No spouse can heal every wound, silence every insecurity, fulfill every longing, remove every loneliness, and make your soul complete.
Eventually, the pedestal collapses.
Not necessarily because they were terrible.
But because they were human.
There is only One who can occupy the throne of your heart without being crushed by the weight of your expectations.
Jesus Christ.
Somebody reading this has been praying desperately for a relationship because loneliness has begun whispering:
“If somebody chooses you, then you'll finally know you're worth loving.”
But the Gospel tells a different story.
Before your future spouse knows your name, Christ knew you.
Before anyone chooses you at an altar, Christ demonstrated His love toward sinners.
Before someone puts a ring on your finger, there was a Savior whose hands were pierced.
Your deepest identity cannot begin with:
“Someone wants me.”
It begins with belonging to Jesus.
That changes dating.
That changes waiting.
That changes rejection.
That changes heartbreak.
Because rejection can still hurt without becoming your identity.
Loneliness can still ache without becoming your master.
You can desire marriage without worshiping marriage.
You can pray for a spouse without treating God like a divine matchmaking service.
You can grieve another relationship that didn't work without concluding that God has forgotten you.
And you can finally stop asking another human being to prove what the cross has already declared:
Christ's love is not something you earned by becoming desirable enough.
It is grace.
Maybe you have made mistakes romantically.
Maybe your story is already messy.
Maybe you gave your heart away recklessly.
Maybe you ignored warning signs because loneliness frightened you more than compromise.
Maybe you stayed because you were terrified nobody else would want you.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once promised yourself you never would.
Maybe you manipulated.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you were cheated on.
Maybe you used someone.
Maybe someone used you.
Maybe you are carrying sexual sin, resentment, shame, bitterness, pornography, emotional dependency, jealousy, or memories you desperately wish you could erase.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not pretending none of it mattered.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace tells the truth about sin...
and then points sinners toward a Savior.
Jesus Christ did not come for people with spotless romantic histories.
He came to save sinners.
Repentance means we stop defending what Christ calls sin and turn toward Him.
And forgiveness does not mean your choices suddenly have no consequences.
It means your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when your life is surrendered to Jesus.
That is the scandal of grace.
Your sin can be real.
Your consequences can be real.
Your wounds can be real.
Your regrets can be real.
And the mercy of Christ can still be greater.
From scandal to grace, Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming sinners through His blood and teaching redeemed people how to live differently.
Maybe that is what God wants to do in your waiting.
Not simply hand you somebody.
Transform you.
Teach you how to tell the truth.
Teach you boundaries.
Teach you purity.
Teach you patience.
Teach you how to communicate instead of manipulate.
Teach you how to apologize.
Teach you how to forgive.
Teach you to recognize unhealthy attachment.
Teach you how to serve.
Teach you how to be alone without believing you are abandoned.
Teach you that “no” can sometimes be mercy.
Teach you that attraction is not discernment.
Teach you that chemistry is not character.
Teach you that somebody quoting Bible verses does not automatically mean they live under the authority of Scripture.
And teach you to stop asking only:
“Do they love God?”
while refusing to ask:
“Does the way they live consistently bear evidence of that confession?”
But turn the question around too.
Does yours?
Because it is dangerously easy to demand spiritual maturity from the person you hope to marry while excusing immaturity in yourself.
“I need someone who communicates.”
Do you?
“I need someone humble.”
Are you?
“I need someone loyal.”
Are you faithful when nobody is watching?
“I need someone emotionally mature.”
Can you receive correction without retaliation?
“I need someone who puts Christ first.”
Does Jesus actually have first place in your own life?
Not your Christian aesthetic.
Not your church attendance.
Not the verse in your bio.
Jesus.
Paul reaches the climax of Colossians 3:14:
ἐπὶ πᾶσιν δὲ τούτοις τὴν ἀγάπην
“And above all these things, love.”
The word is ἀγάπη — agápē.
And Paul calls this love:
σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος — sýndesmos tēs teleiótētos
the bond of completeness, maturity, or perfect unity.
Biblical love is not merely finding someone who gives you butterflies.
Sometimes love is extraordinarily unglamorous.
It listens.
It tells the truth.
It repents.
It forgives.
It serves.
It remains gentle during disagreement.
It refuses manipulation.
It celebrates another person's growth.
It carries burdens.
It chooses faithfulness when feelings fluctuate.
And Christian love ultimately takes its shape from Jesus.

This does not mean you should stay in an abusive or dangerous relationship because you are supposed to “bear with” somebody. Scripture's commands toward patience and forgiveness should never be twisted into permission for abuse, coercion, violence, exploitation, or unrepentant destructive behavior.
Nor does forgiveness automatically mean restored trust.
Trust can require repentance, truth, wisdom, boundaries, and time.
But for ordinary imperfect relationships between imperfect believers, Colossians gives us something our romantic culture desperately needs.
Stop searching for someone who will never inconvenience you.
That person does not exist.
Instead, become deeply rooted in the Christ who can teach two imperfect people to practice compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience, forgiveness, and love.
And here is perhaps the question worth carrying into prayer tonight:
If God gave you the kind of spouse you have been praying for tomorrow, would the person receiving them know how to love them in a Christlike way?
Don't answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Maybe you would.
Maybe there are places where Jesus has already done beautiful work in you.
Thank Him for that.
But maybe the question exposed something.
Pride.
Impatience.
Entitlement.
Fear.
Lust.
Control.
Bitterness.
Unforgiveness.
A desperate need to be chosen.
Don't hide it.
Bring it to Jesus.
Christian conviction is not an invitation to self-hatred.
It is an invitation to repentance and transformation.
The Gospel does not merely say, “Try harder to become marriage material.”
The Gospel says you need Christ.
We cannot manufacture Christlike character merely by becoming more disciplined daters.
We need the grace of God.
We need the Holy Spirit.
We need Scripture.
We need repentance.
We need Christian community.
We need Jesus continually reshaping desires that have become disordered.
So perhaps tonight your prayer does not need to be:
“Jesus, where is my spouse?”
Maybe it needs to become:
“Jesus, make me more like You.
Teach me compassion when selfishness feels easier.
Teach me kindness when irritation rises.
Teach me humility when my pride wants to win.
Teach me gentleness when my words could wound.
Teach me patience when waiting hurts.
Teach me forgiveness because You have forgiven me.
Teach me to love without turning another person into an idol.
And whether marriage comes soon, years from now, or not according to the story I imagined...
do not let me waste this season.
Make me Yours.”
That prayer may not produce an engagement announcement tomorrow.
But it can produce something far more important today:
discipleship.
And if marriage eventually comes, you may discover that the waiting season was never empty.
Jesus was there.
Building things nobody could see.
Removing things nobody else knew were there.
Healing wounds you once expected another person to heal.
Teaching you that being alone and being abandoned are not the same thing.
Teaching you that your relationship status never determined your worth.
Teaching you that marriage is a gift...
but Christ is the treasure.
It does not.
Not because financially supporting a Christian ministry somehow proves that you glorify God. Salvation and God's acceptance cannot be purchased.
But before you leave, remember this:
Maybe the greatest love story being written in your waiting season isn't about the person you're hoping God sends—maybe it is the story of Jesus teaching your heart how to love like His.
